passages.title: Oaths by the dawn and sacred nights
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Fajr 1–5 — Oaths by the Dawn and the Sacred Nights

This passage is a chain of five solemn oaths — by the dawn, the ten nights, the even and the odd, and the departing night — sealed in ayah 5 with a question addressed straight to the intelligent reader: *is this not oath enough for a person of sense?* What binds the five ayat together is that every one of these sworn-by things, on the strongest reading of the early commentators, points to the sacred season of worship at the start of Dhul-Ḥijjah: its dawns, its ten nights, the day of ʿArafah and the Day of Sacrifice. Ibn Kathir sums it up: the oath here is "about the times of worship and the acts of worship themselves, such as Hajj, Salah and other acts of worship" by which Allah's humble servants draw near to Him, seeking His Noble Face.

## The unspoken answer of the oaths

In the Qurʼan an oath exists to certify something. Here, strikingly, the thing being sworn to is not stated in these five ayat — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this is deliberate. The subject of the oaths is implied: it is the truth declared later in the sūrah, *"Surely your Lord is ever on the watch"* (89:14). In other words, the five oaths are marshalled to certify that Allah is watching everything you do, and that reward and punishment for deeds are certain and inevitable. Whoever reflects on the majesty of the things sworn by will find this conclusion "confirmed and verified": everyone must give account, and recompense in the Hereafter is sure. In this connection, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the sūrah then turns (from ayah 6 onward) to the destruction of three previous nations — ʿĀd, Thamūd and Firʿawn — peoples Ibn Kathir describes as rebellious, disobedient, arrogant, outside of Allah's obedience and deniers of His Messengers, whose end was made an exemplary lesson of warning.

## Ayah 1 — "By the dawn"

The early authorities read *al-fajr* in two complementary ways. ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid and as-Suddi took it in its well-known sense: the morning — any dawn. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the daily dawn itself is a sign: it "brings about a great change in the world," turning the mind to the absolute Omnipotence of Allah.

Others held that a specific dawn is meant. Masrūq and Muḥammad bin Kaʿb said it is the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice (an-Naḥr, the 10th of Dhul-Ḥijjah), the last of the ten nights; another narration from Ibn ʿAbbās, shared by Qatādah, refers it to the dawn of the 1st of Muḥarram, the opening of the Islamic year.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Qurtubi) gives a beautiful reason why the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice would deserve an oath of its own. In the Shariʿah, every day is preceded by its own night — except this one. The night before the 10th of Dhul-Ḥijjah belongs, legally, to ʿArafah: a pilgrim who missed standing at ʿArafāt on the 9th may still halt there any time before that dawn breaks, and his Hajj is valid. So the day of ʿArafah has two nights, and the Day of Sacrifice has none — and from this point of view its dawn, among all the days of the year, occupies a special position.

## Ayah 2 — "and the ten nights"

Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Zubayr, Mujāhid and many of the Salaf and later generations agree: these are the first ten nights of Dhul-Ḥijjah. Their worth is established in what Ibn Kathir cites from Sahih Al-Bukhari, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "There are no days in which righteous deeds are more beloved to Allah than these days" — the ten days of Dhul-Ḥijjah. The Companions asked, "Not even fighting Jihad in the way of Allah?" He replied: "Not even Jihad in the way of Allah; except for a man who goes out with his self and his wealth, and he does not return with any of that."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a narration transmitted by Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah — with a chain the commentator himself notes is weak — that a fast on each of these days is equivalent to the fasts of a whole year, and worship on each of these nights is equivalent to worship on the Night of Qadr. Ibn ʿAbbās also connected these ten nights to the story of Mūsā (peace be upon him): *"then We supplemented them with ten"* (7:142) — the same ten nights of Dhul-Ḥijjah, Qurtubi says, were designated for Mūsā. Thus these are the most meritorious ten nights of the whole year.

## Ayah 3 — "and the even and the odd"

The Qurʼan does not itself specify what "the even" (*ash-shafʿ*) and "the odd" (*al-watr*) are, so the commentators differed. The strongest explanation comes in a hadith narrated by Abu-z-Zubair from Jābir, which Ibn Kathir also alludes to: the odd is the day of ʿArafah, because it falls on the ninth, and the even is the Day of Sacrifice, because it falls on the tenth. Qurtubi confirms that this narration's chain is more authentic than the tradition of ʿImrān ibn Ḥusain concerning odd and even units of prayer, and Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah and others preferred this view. On this reading, ayah 3 names by number the two greatest days of the Hajj season whose nights ayah 2 has just sworn by.

A second view, held by Ibn Sīrīn, Masrūq, Abu Ṣāliḥ and Qatādah, widens the lens majestically: "the even" is the entire creation, for Allah says *"And from everything We have created (a pair of) two kinds"* (51:49) — belief and disbelief, light and darkness, night and day, sky and earth, male and female — while "the odd" is Allah alone, the One Being who has no pair: He is Allah, the One, Besought of all, needing none. On this reading the oath sweeps from all of paired creation up to the unpaired Creator Himself.

## Ayah 4 — "and the night when it passes"

The word *yasri* comes from *sarā*, "to travel by night." Here it is the night itself that travels: the ayah swears by the night as it moves away and departs. The early commentators' glosses circle the same meaning. Ibn ʿAbbās said, "when it goes away"; ʿAbdullāh bin Zubayr said, "as some parts of it remove other parts of it"; Mujāhid, Abu al-ʿĀliyah, Qatādah and others said, "when it moves along."

## Ayah 5 — "Is all this not a sufficient oath for those who have sense?"

The key word is *ḥijr*, and it repays attention. Its literal sense is "to prevent." The intellect is called *ḥijr* because it prevents a person from doing or saying what is unbecoming of him. Ibn Kathir traces the same root through the language: the Ḥijr of the Kaʿbah is so named because it prevents the person making Ṭawāf from clinging to the wall facing Ash-Shām; a judge is said to have made *ḥajr* upon someone when his ruling prevents that person from freely disposing of his wealth. The cases differ, but the meaning — restraint — runs through them all.

So the ayah does not merely say "a person of intelligence"; it says a person whose intelligence *restrains* him — one who possesses, in Ibn Kathir's words, "intellect, sound reasoning, understanding and religious discernment." A mind that knows but does not hold its owner back from wrong is not functioning as *ḥijr* at all. And the question form, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is chosen "to awaken man from his slumber": an intelligent person is, in a very special style, invited to think. Are these oaths — the dawn, the ten nights, ʿArafah and the Sacrifice, the departing night — not enough for such a person to accept what they certify: that your Lord is ever on the watch, and the accounting is real?

## Living it

Two practical threads come straight from the sources. First, the hadith in Sahih Al-Bukhari establishes that there are no days in which righteous deeds are more beloved to Allah than the first ten days of Dhul-Ḥijjah. A believer who lets those ten days pass like ordinary days has missed what Allah Himself swore by. Second, this sūrah belongs in the prayer: Ibn Kathir opens his commentary with the incident recorded by An-Nasaʼi, in which the Prophet ﷺ corrected Muʿādh for over-lengthening the congregational prayer — "Are you causing trouble, Muʿādh?" — and named the sūrahs suited to it, among them "By the dawn." A sūrah short enough for the congregation, yet carrying oaths weighty enough to certify the watchfulness of the Lord of the worlds.

passages.title: The destruction of 'Ad, Thamud, and Pharaoh
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the answer to the solemn oaths that open the sūrah. Having sworn by the dawn, the ten nights, the even and the odd, and the departing night — and having asked in ayah 5 whether these are not oath enough "for a man of sense" — Allah now turns to history and presents three exhibits: ʿĀd, Thamūd, and Pharaoh. Three civilisations at the summit of human power, each destroyed. What binds ayat 6–14 together is a single argument: Allah, who dealt with them, is "your Lord," and He is still watching.

## Why these stories follow the oaths

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the logic of the transition. The subject of the opening oaths is implied rather than stated: when a person of intellect reflects on the majesty of the things sworn by, it is confirmed that everyone must give account of his deeds, and that reward and punishment in the Hereafter are certain. The three destroyed nations are cited as proof of exactly this. Indeed, some commentators state that ayah 14 itself — "Surely your Lord is ever on the watch" — is the very subject (the answer) of the five oaths. The whole passage, in other words, is what the sūrah swore to establish.

Ibn Kathir adds a second contrast. He understands the oaths to concern the times and acts of worship — Hajj, Salah, and the devotions of Allah's humble, obedient servants. Immediately after mentioning those pious worshippers, Allah mentions their opposites: peoples who were rebellious, arrogant, deniers of His Messengers and rejectors of His Scriptures — so He destroyed them, annihilated them, and "made them legends to be spoken of and an exemplary lesson of warning."

Notice too how the question is framed in ayah 6: "Did you not see how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd?" — not merely "Allah," but *your* Lord. The One who judged those tyrants is the same Lord you stand before.

## ʿĀd — Iram of the pillars (ayat 6–8)

**Who they were.** Ibn Kathir, citing Ibn Ishaq, identifies them as the first people of ʿĀd, descendants of ʿĀd bin Iram bin ʿAws bin Sām bin Nūḥ. Allah sent them His Messenger Hūd; they rejected and opposed him, so Allah saved Hūd and the believers with him and destroyed the rest with a furious, violent wind — the wind described elsewhere in the Qurʼān as imposed on them "for seven nights and eight days in succession," leaving them "as if they were hollow trunks of date palms" (69:7–8). Their story is told in more than one place in the Qurʼān, Ibn Kathir notes, so that the believers may learn a lesson from their demise.

**Why "Iram"?** Grammatically, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, "Iram" in ayah 7 stands in apposition to ʿĀd (as an explicative or complement): it specifies *which* ʿĀd is meant — ʿĀd al-ūlā, the earlier generation, called "the earlier ʿĀd" in 53:50, who are linked most closely to their forefather Iram. The early authorities differed on the word's exact reference: Mujahid said Iram was an ancient nation, the first people of ʿĀd; Qatadah and as-Suddi said it refers to the House of the kingdom of ʿĀd — a view Ibn Kathir calls "good and strong."

**"Of the pillars" (dhāt al-ʿimād).** The word *ʿimād* means pillar, and the commentators read the epithet in two complementary ways. Ibn Kathir: they lived in trellised houses raised on firm pillars, and were the strongest people of their time in physique and might. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: they are "the men of tall pillars" because they themselves were towering in stature — stronger and more powerful than any other nation. Their strength was a divine gift, and that is precisely how their Prophet appealed to them: Hūd reminded them that Allah had made them successors after the people of Nūḥ and "increased you amply in stature" (7:69), directing them to spend that power in obedience to the One who created them. Instead they boasted, "Who is mightier than us in strength?" — to which the Qurʼān replies, "See they not that Allah Who created them was mightier in strength than them?" (41:15).

**"The like of which were not created in the land" (ayah 8).** Whom does "the like of which" describe? Ibn Zayd took it to refer to the pillars — structures so lofty that nothing like them had been built. Qatadah and Ibn Jarir took it to refer to the tribe itself: no people like them, in strength and stature, had been created in their time. Ibn Kathir rules for the latter and calls Ibn Zayd's view weak, with a sharp linguistic argument: had buildings been meant, Allah would have said "the like of which were not *produced*"; but He said "not *created* (lam yukhlaq)" — a verb suited to people, not masonry.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note of scholarly restraint here. The Qurʼān affirms that this nation was unmatched in physical stature but deliberately gives no measurements — that detail was unnecessary for its purpose. The fantastic figures in circulation (a report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil that they were eighteen feet tall) appear to derive from Israelite traditions and are difficult to believe; and Allah knows best. The same work records a minority interpretation, cited from Qurtubi, that "Iram" was the name of an artificial "paradise" built by Shaddād, a son of ʿĀd — a lofty structure on tall pillars of gold and silver, studded with jewels, built so that people might prefer a ready-made paradise over the Paradise of the Hereafter; when Shaddād and his nobles came to enter it, divine punishment overtook and destroyed them all. On that reading the verse points to one specific punishment; but the majority of commentators prefer the first reading, in which the passage covers all the punishments that fell upon ʿĀd.

## Thamūd — who cut the rock (ayah 9)

Thamūd "hewed (jābū) the rocks in the valley." Ibn ʿAbbās said: they carved them and hewed them — and Mujahid, Qatadah, ad-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said the same. Ibn Kathir lingers on the word: from this root Arabic speaks of the "hewing" of a leopard skin when it is torn and of a garment when it is cut open, and from it comes *jayb*, the opening or pocket of a garment. The image is of a people who could slice through solid stone as easily as cloth — the Qurʼān says of them elsewhere, "And you hew in the mountains, houses with great skill" (26:149). Where ʿĀd's glory was raised up in pillars, Thamūd's was carved down into rock. Neither protected them.

## Pharaoh — the man of the stakes (ayah 10)

Firʿawn is called *dhū al-awtād*, "the man of the awtād" — *awtād* being the plural of *watad*, a peg, stake or nail. The early authorities gave two explanations. Al-ʿAwfi reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the awtād were his armies, who enforced his commands for him — power itself as the "pegs" that held his tyranny fast. Mujahid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, al-Hasan and as-Suddi said he used to nail people up on pegs: driving stakes of iron through hands and feet and hanging his victims from them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, noting that the majority of commentators hold the torture explanation, fills in the horror: he would hammer stakes into the ground and bind people to them, or pin them by their hands and feet to lie in the scorching sun, left to the mercy of snakes and scorpions. Some commentators recount that he inflicted this same torture on his own wife ʾĀsiyah when she embraced faith and declared it to him, and so destroyed her [as related in Mazhari].

## The shared indictment and the shared end (ayat 11–13)

Ayat 11–12 gather all three under one charge: "they transgressed beyond bounds in the lands, and made therein much mischief" — in Ibn Kathir's words, they rebelled, were arrogant, and went about spreading corruption in the land and *harming the people*. The crime the Qurʼān names is not their architecture or their strength; it is tyranny and the injury of Allah's servants.

So, ayah 13: "Your Lord poured on them a whip (sawt) of torment." Both commentaries open up this striking metaphor. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the torment is called a whip because, just as lashes are inflicted across different parts of the body, the punishment these nations received was similar to it in that they suffered different kinds of punishment. Ibn Kathir adds the force of the verb *ṣabba*, "poured": torment sent down upon them from the sky, a punishment that could not be repelled from a criminal people.

## "Your Lord is ever on the watch" (ayah 14)

The passage closes with its point. The word *mirṣād* comes from a root meaning to lie in wait or keep watch; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that it denotes a place of ambush or observation — classically, a narrow pass that travellers must come through while someone waits for them there. No one should imagine he can slip past divine justice: all are under Allah's authority and power, and He may administer His punishment whenever He wills.

Ibn ʿAbbās explained the ayah simply: "He hears and He sees." We affirm this as the Salaf did — Allah truly hears and truly sees, without likening Him to His creation and without explaining the words away. Ibn Kathir draws out what it means: Allah watches over His creation in all that they do, and will reward them in this life and the Hereafter according to what each of them strove for. He will bring the whole creation before Him and judge them with justice, giving each exactly what he deserves — for He is far removed from injustice and tyranny.

That last phrase is the quiet consolation inside the warning. The Lord who lies in wait for tyrants is a Lord of perfect justice. For every believer who hears this sūrah, the destruction of ʿĀd, Thamūd, and Pharaoh is not merely a threat but a promise: no pillar, no rock-hewn fortress, no army of stakes has ever put its owners beyond the reach of your Lord. The believers are meant, as Ibn Kathir says, to take these nations as an exemplary lesson: strength is a grace from Allah, and it is answered for — either spent in His obedience, as Hūd urged ʿĀd, or requited by the One who is ever watchful.

passages.title: Misreading wealth as honor, poverty as disgrace
passages.tafsir:
This passage corrects one of the deepest and most instinctive errors in the human reading of life: the assumption that wealth signals Allah's acceptance and poverty His rejection. Ayat 15–16 state the error in the voice of the one who makes it; ayah 17 shatters it with a single word, *kallā* — "No, never!" — and ayat 17–20 then turn the tables, exposing what the wealthy are actually doing with the wealth they mistook for honor.

## The false equation (ayat 15–16)

In ayah 15, "man" — *al-insān* — is given honor and bounties by his Lord and concludes, "My Lord has honored me." In ayah 16, his provision is straitened and he protests, "My Lord has disgraced me." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that "man" here refers primarily to the unbelieving man, who may form any thought about Allah as he pleases — but in its general sense the word can include a Muslim who slips into the very same assumption. It is regrettable, the commentary notes, that many Muslims today fall into similar ideas.

Notice what both halves of the verse actually say before the man speaks: *ibtalāhu rabbuhu* — "his Lord **tests** him." The Qur'an names the reality (test) before quoting the man's misreading of it (honor, disgrace). Whether the test comes wrapped in bounty or in restriction, it is the same word: *ibtilāʼ*, trial. The man sees two opposite verdicts; Allah declares one continuous examination.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies two false ideas the devil plants in the person showered with wealth and health. First, he grows haughty and credits his own superior intellect, capability, and effort. Second, he assumes he must enjoy a favorable status with Allah — otherwise, why the abundance? And when provision is curtailed, the same logic runs in reverse: he takes poverty as a curse and complains that Allah is humiliating him when he deserved honor.

## Kallā — "No, never!" (ayah 17)

Allah's answer is one emphatic word: *kallā*. Ibn Kathir explains: the matter is not as he claims, neither in this nor in that. **Allah gives wealth to those whom He loves and to those whom He does not love; and He withholds provision from those whom He loves and from those whom He does not love.** Wealth is simply not a signal of divine acceptance, and poverty is not a signal of rejection. The point, Ibn Kathir says, is that Allah should be obeyed in either circumstance: the wealthy man thanks Him; the poor man exercises patience.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the refutation further — often the matter is quite the contrary. Firʿaun (Pharaoh) claimed godhood and lordship, yet never suffered so much as a headache. Some of the Prophets (peace be upon them) were sawn in two by their enemies. So much for the claim that ease is honor and hardship disgrace.

The same commentary cites two reports of the Prophet ﷺ. He is reported to have said that the poor refugees will enter Paradise forty years before the wealthy muhājirs (Immigrants) — Imam Muslim transmitted it from ʿAbdullah Ibn ʿUmar, as cited in Maẓharī. And in another narration he is reported to have said that whomever Allah loves, He keeps away from worldly luxuries just as people keep their sick away from water — transmitted by Ahmad and Tirmidhi on the authority of Qatādah Ibn Nuʿmān, as cited in Maẓharī. Far from proving disgrace, restricted provision can itself be a mark of divine care.

## The turn: what you actually do with wealth (ayat 17–20)

Having said *kallā*, the passage pivots with *bal* — "But" / "In fact" — and the pronoun shifts from "he" to **you**. The complainers are now addressed directly, and four charges follow. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the first of them as a rebuff to those who think wealth is an "honor" and poverty a "dishonor" — and it suggests, further, that their provision is straitened *because* they squander wealth in immoral pursuits and strip the orphans of their rights in it.

**First charge — "you are not gracious to the orphan" (ayah 17).** The wording matters. The underlying failure is that they deprive orphans of their rights and do not spend on them what is due — yet the verse does not say "you do not *pay* the orphan" but "you do not *honor* (tukrimūn) the orphan." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why: gratitude to Allah, and simple humanity, demand more than transferring money. The orphan must be honored — treated with dignity and kindness. A guardian must not despise his ward or look down on him, and must not discriminate between the orphan and his own children. Money without respect fails the test. Ibn Kathir notes that the verse contains a command to honor the orphan, and cites what Abu Dawud recorded from Sahl bin Saʿid: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "The guardian of the orphan and I will be like these two in Paradise," and he put his middle and index fingers together.

**Second charge — "nor do you urge one another to feed the poor" (ayah 18).** The verb here is not "you do not feed" but "you do not *urge one another* (taḥāḍḍūn)." Ibn Kathir: they neither command that the poor be treated kindly nor encourage each other to do so. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws two duties from this phrasing. The style of the verse indicates that the affluent are obligated to spend on the poor from their own wealth — but it also means that even the person who has nothing to give is not excused: the poor cannot spend for lack of means, yet they should at least encourage others to feed the needy.

**Third charge — "you devour inheritance greedily" (ayah 19).** The Arabic is *taʼkulūna at-turātha aklan lammā* — literally devouring the inheritance with a devouring that is *lamm*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the word: *lamm* means to gather, amass, and concentrate — a sweeping gulp. Ibn Kathir: they devour it however they can get it, lawful or forbidden. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān paints the scene: when someone dies, they take their own share and the shares of others along with it — shares belonging to orphans, widows, or heirs who are absent. And it asks why, of all wealth, *inheritance* was singled out. Because having a greedy eye on a dead man's estate is proof of a man's greed and voracity for wealth: he stares at the wealth of the dying "like a beast of prey," waiting for the person to die so the estate can be carved up. An honorable person of principle would not look at the deceased's wealth with greedy eyes. (The commentary adds the general rule in passing: mixing lawful and forbidden wealth is not permitted in any transaction.)

**Fourth charge — "and you love wealth fervently" (ayah 20).** The word *jamm* means "excessive." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a precise and merciful distinction from this single qualifier: the verse does not condemn loving wealth as such — a sober love of wealth is a natural human instinct, and it is not what is denounced here. What is condemned is the *excessive*, insatiable love, love without limit. Ibn Kathir adds that this abundance of love increases some people in wickedness.

## Reading the passage whole

Ibn Kathir frames both halves of the passage under one heading: wealth and poverty are both a test. He cites Allah's words elsewhere: "Do they think that in wealth and children with which We enlarge them, We hasten unto them with good things? Nay, but they perceive not" (23:55–56). Abundance is not accelerated reward; it is examination material. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, as noted above, reads the charge about the orphan as a rebuff aimed precisely at those who equate wealth with honor: they claim honor for themselves on account of wealth, while withholding honor from the orphan to whom Allah commanded it be given.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes where the sūrah goes next: after listing these four traits, the passage returns to the theme sworn to by the five oaths at the sūrah's opening — the punishment of the Hereafter — beginning with the earth being crushed "*dakkan dakkā*" (ayah 21). The indictment of ayat 15–20 is not left hanging; it is heading toward the end of the world and the Day of Resurrection.

## Living it

The sources leave the believer with a concrete standard. In wealth: gratitude, not self-congratulation — and no inference that Allah is pleased with you. In hardship: patience, not the complaint "my Lord has disgraced me" — and no inference that Allah has rejected you; restricted provision can itself be a mark of divine care. Toward the orphan: money *and* dignity — no condescension, no favoring your own children over a ward. Toward the hungry: feed them if you can; urge others to feed them even if you cannot. Toward inheritance: hands off every share that is not yours, and no waiting on a relative's death with a calculating eye. Toward wealth itself — *al-māl*: love it as the natural instinct allows, but never *ḥubban jammā* — never with the limitless, excessive love the verse condemns.

passages.title: The Day the earth is crushed and Hell arrives
passages.tafsir:
This passage is Surah al-Fajr's answer to everything that came before it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that after cataloguing the evil traits of the unbelievers — culminating in their excessive, insatiable love of wealth — the surah turns back to the main theme it opened with, the theme its five opening oaths were sworn for: the punishment of the Hereafter. It does so first by describing the end of the world, and then the establishment of the Day of Resurrection. Ayat 21–26 are one continuous scene, and it moves without pause: the earth is pounded flat, the Lord comes with the angels in ranks, Hell is brought near, and only then — too late — does man finally understand.

## The scene unfolds

The passage opens with **kallā** — rendered "Enough!" or "Nay!" — which Ibn Kathir glosses simply as meaning *truly*. Enough of the love of wealth; truly, here is where it all leads.

*When the earth is crushed, dakkan dakkā.* The key word is **dakk**, which, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, literally means to pound or crush a thing into bits and pieces. This refers to the earthquakes that will crush and grind the mountains to dust; the world itself will be dissolved. And the word is *repeated* — *dakkan dakkā*, "crushed, crushed" — which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads as showing that there will be a whole **series** of earthquakes before the dissolution of the world. The English "crushed over and over" is trying to carry that drumbeat repetition of the Arabic. Ibn Kathir describes the result: the earth and the mountains will be flattened, levelled and made even, and from that levelled plain the creatures will rise from their graves for their Lord. The demolition of the world and the raising of the dead are two halves of one event: this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is the first stage of Resurrection, and when it ends, the second stage begins.

*And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank.* Here the two commentaries each speak with care, and each leaves the "how" entirely with Allah. Ibn Kathir says that Allah will come for the session of Judgement between His creatures **"as He wills"** — affirming the coming while committing its manner to Him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls the words "your Lord will come" an allegorical expression, and states plainly: **"No one, besides Allah, knows the nature of His coming."** The angels' arrival, by contrast, is — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it — clear in meaning: they will arrive in the Plain of Gathering lined up in rows upon rows before Him — *ṣaffan ṣaffā*, another doubled word, rank behind rank.

**The intercession that opens the Judgement.** Ibn Kathir sets this ayah inside one of the most moving scenes of the Last Day. The Lord's coming for judgement happens after mankind — desperate for the reckoning to simply *begin* — has gone to the great Messengers one after another, begging each to intercede with Allah. Every one of them will answer, "I cannot do that for you." The beseeching will continue until it reaches the best of the Sons of Adam, Muhammad ﷺ, and he will say, **"I will do it, I will do it."** He will go and seek to intercede with Allah, and Allah will allow him to intercede for the Judgement to commence. Ibn Kathir notes that this will be the *first* of the intercessions, and that it is the **praiseworthy station** already discussed in Surat Subhan (al-Isrāʼ). So behind the terse words "and your Lord comes" lies an entire drama: creation pleading, every prophet stepping back, and one man ﷺ stepping forward for all of humanity.

*And Hell is brought forth on that Day.* Not merely uncovered — **brought**. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith recorded by Imam Muslim bin Al-Hajjaj in his Sahih, from ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"Hell will be brought on near that Day and it will have seventy thousand leashes, and each leash will have seventy thousand angels pulling it."** At-Tirmidhi also recorded the same narration. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that no one besides Allah knows how exactly Hell will be brought forward in the Plain of Gathering, but offers this picture: Hell, which is at present beneath the seventh earth, will at that moment flare up, the oceans will become part of its flame, and it will stand in front of the entire gathering — visible to all.

## The realisation that comes too late

*This is when man will remember — but how will that remembrance avail him?* Ibn Kathir explains: he will remember his deeds, what he did in times past and recent. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unlocks the word: **tadhakkur** here means *to realise*. The unbelievers will finally realise the errors of their ways in the Hereafter — but too late, "because it is this present world where īmān (faith) and good deeds benefit the people. The Hereafter is the place only for reckoning and retribution." The rhetorical question — "but from where will he take advantage of such realisation?" — is the Qurʼān's own bitter answer: from nowhere.

The realisation bursts out as a cry: *Yā laytanī qaddamtu li-ḥayātī* — "Alas! Would that I had sent forth for my life!" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the moment: facing the torment of disbelief and idolatry on that day of devastation, man will lament that he should have carried out good deeds and refrained from sin in this world, to be saved from punishment in the Hereafter. But it will be of no avail.

Ibn Kathir draws out a sobering breadth in this regret: **it will not belong to the sinners alone.** If a person was disobedient, he will be sorry for the acts of disobedience he committed. But if he was *obedient*, he will wish that he had performed more acts of obedience. Ibn Kathir supports this with what Imam Ahmad bin Hanbal recorded from Muhammad bin Abi ʿAmirah, one of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "If a servant fell down on his face (in prostration) from the day that he was born until the day he died as an old man, in obedience to Allah, he would scorn this act on the Day of Judgement. He would wish to be returned to this life so that he could earn more reward and compensation." A whole lifetime spent in prostration — and even that will look small once the reward is actually seen. If the obedient will feel they did too little, what of those who did nothing?

## A punishment and a binding like no other

The passage closes on two parallel declarations: *So on that Day none will punish as He will punish, and none will bind as He will bind.* Ibn Kathir explains: there is no one more severely punished than those whom Allah punishes for disobeying Him, and no one more severely punished and bound than the disbelievers whom az-Zabāniyah punish. And he adds a clause that matters: **this is for the criminals and the wrongdoers among the creatures.** The threat is targeted, not universal — the terror of this scene falls on those who earned it.

## Living it

The passage's own logic tells the believer what to do with it. The regret of the cry "would that I had sent forth for my life" is placed before us *now*, while sending something forth is still possible — because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, it is this present world where faith and good deeds benefit people; the Hereafter is the place only for reckoning and retribution. And the report of Muhammad bin Abi ʿAmirah quietly removes the excuse of the already-religious: if a lifetime of prostration will seem too little on that Day, then no one alive has yet done "enough." The response this passage asks for is not despair but urgency — to send forth today what you will desperately wish for then.

passages.title: The tranquil soul welcomed into Paradise
passages.tafsir:
## The most beautiful words a soul will ever hear

These four short ayat are the words with which Allah welcomes the soul of the believer — first calling it by the loveliest of names, "O tranquil soul," then inviting it back to its Lord, into the company of His righteous servants, and finally into His own Paradise. They close Surah al-Fajr, and they are inseparable from what comes immediately before them: ayat 21–26 described the terror of the Day when the earth is pounded flat, when the Lord comes for the session of Judgement with the angels in rows, when Hell itself is dragged near, and when the heedless man cries, "Would that I had sent forth for my life!" Against that backdrop of a punishment and binding "like none other," Ibn Kathir says the address turns to "the pure and tranquil soul — which is always at rest and abiding by the truth."

## "O tranquil soul" — what an-nafs al-mutmaʾinnah means

Everything in ayah 27 turns on one word: *muṭmaʾinnah*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that it literally means "calm" — the soul that has become peaceful and tranquil **as a result of the remembrance and obedience of Allah**, so much so that when the believer abandons remembrance, he feels restless. The commentary then adds, carefully, that this is *probably* the same soul that has been made pure, through spiritual exercises and discipline, from evil traits and bad conduct — the soul for whom obedience to Allah and His remembrance have become a predisposition, and the Shariʿah has become, as it were, its very nature. Tranquility here is not a mood or a temperament; it is the settled state of a soul whose whole orientation is towards its Lord. Ibn Kathir's description matches: it is the soul "always at rest and abiding by the truth."

## "Return to your Lord" — a homecoming, not a departure

In ayah 28 the soul is not told "go" but "come back" — *irjiʿī*, return. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the tenderness of this choice of word: it indicates that the soul's *first* place was with its Lord, and it is now being commanded to go back to Him. This, the commentary notes, accords with the narration that the souls of the believers, together with their Book of Deeds, rest in *ʿIlliyyīn* — a place on the seventh heaven in the shade of the Throne of the Most-Merciful — the original resting-place of human souls, from which they are placed into bodies and to which the believing soul returns after death. Death, for such a soul, is a homecoming.

Ibn Kathir explains the return "to your Lord" as a return to His company, His reward, and what He has prepared for His servants in His Paradise.

## "Well-pleased and well-pleasing" — a mutual pleasure

The two words *rāḍiyah marḍiyyah* in ayah 28 describe a relationship flowing in both directions. Ibn Kathir: the soul is well-pleased "within itself," and pleased with Allah — and He is pleased with it and will gratify it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds this further: the believer's soul is well-pleased with the decrees Allah destined for it *and* with His legislative commands — contentment with what Allah has done and with what Allah has asked — and Allah in turn is well-pleased with His slave. It then adds a point of real practical weight: the slave's being pleased with Allah's decrees and injunctions is itself **a sign** that Allah is pleased with him. If you want to know where you stand with Allah, look at how your heart receives His decree and His command.

## First among My servants, then into My Paradise

The order of ayat 29 and 30 is deliberate, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān dwells on it. The soul is *first* told "enter among My servants" and only *then* "enter My Paradise." This indicates that entry into Paradise depends, first and foremost, on being within the fold of the righteous believers — they will then enter Paradise all together. And it teaches something for this life: keeping the company of the righteous in this world is a sign that one will enter Paradise with them. The commentary reminds us that this companionship is so precious that even the Prophets prayed for it — Sulaiman (peace be upon him) prayed, "admit me, by Your mercy, among Your righteous slaves" (27:19), and Yusuf (peace be upon him) prayed, "make me join the righteous" (12:101). A blessing the Prophets themselves asked for is not one we can afford to neglect.

Then comes the crown of the passage. In ayah 30 Allah does not simply say "enter Paradise" but "enter **My** Paradise" — *jannatī*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on this attribution: it is a great honour, and it indicates that Paradise is not only a place of every eternal comfort, but above all a place of Allah's pleasure. What makes Paradise Paradise is that it is *His*.

## When are these words spoken?

The scholars discussed when the soul hears this address, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the views fairly. Some commentators say it is spoken on the Day of Reckoning, after the reckoning is over — and the context supports this, since the preceding ayat describe the punishment of the disbelievers in the Hereafter. Other scholars hold that the believer is addressed in this world, at the time of death, and many authentic traditions bear this out. Ibn Kathir reconciles the two: Allah will address the soul of the believer with these words **twice** — once at the time of death, and again on the Day of Judgement — just as the angels give glad tidings to the believer both when he dies and when he rises from his grave.

Among the traditions supporting the address at death, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a lengthy narration of Abu Hurairah, recorded in the Musnad of Ahmad, Nasa'i and Ibn Majah, in which the Prophet ﷺ said that when death approaches a believer, the angels of mercy bring him a piece of white silk and say: "Come out [from this body], well-pleased and well-pleasing, to Divine mercy and to the eternal comforts of Paradise."

## Abu Bakr and the promise of this ayah

Each commentary preserves a report — framed somewhat differently — in which Abu Bakr hears this ayah in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ and is promised its glad tidings. Ibn Kathir relates, from the report of Ibn Abi Hatim on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, that this ayah was revealed while Abu Bakr was sitting with the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Bakr said, "O Messenger of Allah! There is nothing better than this!" The Prophet ﷺ replied: **"This will indeed be said to you."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, for its part, records Ibn ʿAbbas recounting that one day he himself recited the verse "O contented soul" in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ; Abu Bakr, who was present in the assembly, said, "O Allah's Messenger, what a fine address and honour!" — and the Prophet ﷺ told him, "Behold, the angel will address you thus after your death." Whether at the moment of revelation or at a later recitation, the promise is the same: the first man to marvel at this ayah was assured that he would hear it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also relates, under the heading "A Few Strange Incidents," reports of these ayat surfacing at the deaths of the righteous: Saʿid ibn Jubair's account that when Ibn ʿAbbas passed away in Taʾif, an invisible voice was heard reciting "O tranquil soul…" from the side of his grave; and an incident recorded by Hafiz Tabarani in his Kitab-ul-ʿAjaʾib of a Muslim prisoner in a Roman city who was beheaded for refusing to renounce his faith — his severed head, cast into the river, rose to the surface and recited these four ayat to the three companions who had apostatized under threat, whereupon they returned to Islam and the Christians of that place embraced it in great numbers.

## Living toward this address

The passage itself tells us how a soul comes to hear these words. Tranquility grows from remembrance and obedience of Allah; pleasure with Allah's decree and command is cultivated now, and is itself the sign of His pleasure; and the company of the righteous is sought in this world, because entering Paradise "among My servants" begins with standing among them here. The surah has shown us the man who will cry "Would that I had sent forth for my life!" — and, in these closing ayat, the soul for whom no regret remains: welcomed home to its Lord, well-pleased, well-pleasing, among His servants, in His Paradise.
